passage:
Devika could not sleep. At a dinner she had let slip that Sarita was laid off in March, something Sarita had told her in confidence, and it was already spreading. She rang Sarita before anyone else could. "I repeated your secret to people at dinner. I am sorry. No excuses. If you need distance, I will give it."

Sarita's ears burned, humiliation and rage in equal parts. "That was mine to tell," she said. "When Aditi asked about my job hunt I felt exposed." Then she stopped and waited. Devika did not argue. She wrote to each person she had told, asked them to let it go, and stayed quietly available for two weeks. Sarita watched the repair, not the excuses, and it decided her. A month later they met for tea.

Meanwhile Siddharth confided over coffee that he was seeing someone behind his partner's back. Sarita's chest tightened. "I won't lie for you, and I think you should tell her yourself," she said. She did not post about it or cut him off.

And an old flatmate who rang only when short of cash or needing a sofa got a different answer that month: "I can lend this once, but not again soon." Sarita hung up without a long explanation, knowing a friendship with no care running both ways stays thin.

qa.q: When had Sarita been laid off?
qa.a: Sarita was laid off in March.

qa.q: How did Devika's and Sarita's handling of the leaked secret compare with Sarita's handling of Siddharth's confidence?
qa.a: Devika told Sarita first, apologised without excuses and offered distance, and Sarita said clearly how it felt and judged by the repair. When Siddharth confided, Sarita refused to lie for him and told him honestly what she thought, without exposing him or cutting him off.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel when Aditi asked about her job hunt?
qa.a: She felt exposed, humiliated and full of rage.

qa.q: What did Sarita do about the old flatmate who rang only when in need?
qa.a: She offered to lend once, said no to more without a long explanation, and did not pretend the friendship was close.

grounding: A leaked secret is seen from the person hurt and the person who repeated it, beside a friend's confided wrongdoing and a friend who only calls to take.

passage:
Salma's dog Moti did not wake up on Monday, and by afternoon Salma was on the rug with her face wet. "Where did Moti go? When is he coming back?" Her mother, Nazia, sat down and pulled her close. "Moti died, sweetheart. His body stopped working and he will not come back. It is okay to be sad. We loved him very much." Salma cried harder, but her shoulders loosened. Nazia did not tell her to stop, or promise a new puppy.

At bedtime Salma whispered, "I forgot his dinner once. And I shouted at him." Nazia held her face. "It was not because of anything you did, Salma. Not one thing."

On Tuesday Salma drew Moti with a big red ball, and with her mother laid the picture under his favourite tree to say goodbye.

At school, Nandini heard the news. "It's just a dog. You can get another." Salma's tummy hurt. She said, in a small voice, "He was my friend." Nandini blinked and said, "Oh." Salma told Mummy that night, and Nazia said gently, "Some children don't know what to say yet. Maybe we can teach them words like 'I'm sorry he died.'" The next day Nandini brought a drawing of a flower.

qa.q: Where did Salma and her mother lay the picture of Moti?
qa.a: They laid it under his favourite tree.

qa.q: How did Nazia's answers differ from Nandini's remark, and how did each land on Salma?
qa.a: Nazia named the death plainly, said sadness was okay and lifted the blame, so Salma's shoulders loosened. Nandini's "just a dog" brushed the loss aside and hurt her tummy, until Salma said "He was my friend."

qa.q: Why did Salma whisper about forgetting Moti's dinner and shouting at him?
qa.a: She felt guilty and afraid that her forgetting and shouting might be why Moti died.

qa.q: How could an adult help Nandini learn what to say to a grieving friend?
qa.a: They could teach gentle words like "I'm sorry he died", as Nazia suggested.

grounding: A child's grief for a dog, a parent's plain comfort, a friend's dismissive remark and a child's fear that she caused the death are shown together.

passage:
Rashmi heard the whisper at the water tap: her parents had been shouting at home, and someone's cousin had seen. By lunch the whole class seemed to know. Her ears burned and she wished the floor would open. Then she told herself it was not her fault, and at recess she went to her class teacher, who listened, said so too, and spoke to the whole class after lunch about unkind stories. Asha, her friend since first grade, sat beside her all week.

Deepak had leaned in at the tap, hungry for details, because whispering made him feel part of the group. Then he saw Rashmi's face across the room and thought: what if it were my house? When Imran passed him a fresh rumour, he said, "How would you feel if they said that about you?" and asked about the cricket match instead.

Vaibhav's friends wanted him to join a chat laughing at Rashmi. His stomach tightened; if he stayed out, they might turn on him next. He wrote, "I'm not into this," politely, and put his phone away. On Friday he sat with Deepak and Rashmi at lunch and was surprised at how easy it felt.

qa.q: Where did Rashmi first hear the whisper?
qa.a: She heard it at the water tap.

qa.q: How did Deepak's first reaction to the whispers differ from his second, and what did Vaibhav's fear lead him to do?
qa.a: At first Deepak leaned in for details because whispering felt like belonging. Then he pictured his own house and asked how they would feel if it were said about them, and steered away. Vaibhav, afraid he might be next, stayed polite, stayed out and later sat with Rashmi.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she realised the whole class knew?
qa.a: She felt exposed and ashamed, wishing the floor would open.

qa.q: What helped Rashmi after the rumour spread?
qa.a: She told her class teacher, who listened and spoke to the class that afternoon, and Asha stayed beside her all week.

grounding: One rumour about a classmate's family is met by the girl who is talked about, a curious child who turns to empathy, and a child who fears being next.

passage:
Before the science test, Sahil and three others crowded Anand's desk. "Just show us the answers, don't be selfish." Anand's neck went hot. "No, but I will study with you tonight," he said, and Sahil scowled for the rest of the day.

On Friday, Suraj pulled him behind the bicycle shed. "I copied from a guide in the maths test. Please keep it to yourself." Anand listened without a lecture. "I can't say it's okay," he said. "You should tell the teacher yourself, before it grows." Suraj shrugged and walked off.

On Monday the teacher stood before the class. "Someone used unfair help on the maths test. Anyone who knows something, come and see me privately." Anand's stomach twisted all through the lesson. Honest students had worked hard, and yet Suraj was his friend. He did not whisper in the corridor or lie. After the last bell he told the teacher what he knew.

By Wednesday, Suraj's group had stopped saving Anand a seat, and he heard "snitch" behind his back. It hurt, and he felt like a traitor, but he stayed steady. He sat with Sahil, who had come round after the study evening, and two others who shared their tiffin.

qa.q: Where did Suraj tell Anand about the cheating?
qa.a: Suraj told him behind the bicycle shed.

qa.q: How did Sahil react to Anand's honesty compared with how Suraj reacted?
qa.a: Sahil scowled after Anand refused to show the answers but came round after the study evening and sat with him, while Suraj shrugged and walked off when told to tell the teacher, and later Suraj's group stopped saving Anand a seat.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling during the lesson after the teacher asked who knew something?
qa.a: He felt torn. His stomach twisted because honest students had worked hard, yet Suraj was his friend.

qa.q: What helped Anand cope after Suraj's group turned on him?
qa.a: He stayed steady and sat with Sahil and two others who shared their tiffin.

grounding: One teenager meets pressure to share answers, a friend's secret about cheating, a teacher's direct question, and the cost of reporting.

passage:
Swati had two bosses in her first job. Damini, her manager, went through her drafts with her every Friday. Swati asked, "What would you change?", owned a mistake in a client sheet, and brought two ways to fix it. Damini nodded. "Good. I will take the second."

Suraj, the department head, was different. Some days he barked at the room, other days he joked. Swati went quiet in his meetings, heart thudding. Then she started jotting her points the night before and sending updates by email, and stopped reading his frowns as a verdict on her.

But Suraj also kept asking her to stay late, unpaid, with lines like "there might be a bonus in it." By the third week of nine o'clock exits she recognised the pattern. She told Damini, who agreed the hours were not fair. Swati wrote down her days and told Suraj politely that she could stay late only when it was agreed in writing. She also asked a senior friend outside the company for advice.

Meanwhile a colleague was named star of the month for a pitch Swati had wanted. Her stomach curdled. She did not whisper about it. She asked what he had done, borrowed the way he laid out his deck, and kept to her own pace.

qa.q: When did Damini go through Swati's drafts?
qa.a: Damini went through her drafts every Friday.

qa.q: How did Damini's way of managing differ from Suraj's?
qa.a: Damini went through Swati's drafts every Friday and agreed the unpaid hours were not fair, while Suraj swung between barking and joking and kept asking Swati to stay late unpaid with hints of a bonus.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling in Suraj's meetings?
qa.a: She felt fear and dread. Her heart thudded and she went quiet.

qa.q: How did Swati turn her envy of the colleague into something useful?
qa.a: She asked what he had done, borrowed the way he laid out his deck, and kept her own pace without whispering about him.

grounding: A first job brings a guiding manager, a moody department head, unpaid late nights with vague promises, and a colleague's recognition, all handled by one newcomer.

passage:
Akash said "pasghetti" for spaghetti, and the whole class giggled. His face went hot and he shrank in his chair. "That is unkind," he said in a small voice. The teacher came over. "Everyone here is still learning words." Akash tried again, slowly, and this time someone laughed with him, not at him.

That afternoon Pankaj stopped playing, stood very still, and his shorts were wet. His face burned, tears rolling, and he wished he could vanish. The teacher came quietly, handed him a fresh pair in a bag, walked him to the toilets and said nothing to the class. "It was an accident, and lots of children have them." Pankaj stopped crying.

On Saturday Hafsa visited a guest's house and tipped juice over a cream sofa. Her lip trembled. Mama said, "Accidents happen. Let's clean up together." They wiped it side by side and Hafsa felt light again.

On Monday a different teacher made Hafsa stand and show her sum to the class as the wrong one. Her cheeks flamed and her eyes stung. At home she told Mama. Mama hugged her, said it was not her fault, and phoned the school that same evening to ask for a talk with the head.

qa.q: What did Akash say for spaghetti?
qa.a: Akash said "pasghetti".

qa.q: How did the two teachers' actions differ, and how did that affect the children?
qa.a: One teacher helped Pankaj quietly and said it was an accident, so Pankaj stopped crying. The other made Hafsa stand and show her mistake to the class, leaving her cheeks flaming and needing Mama's help.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when his shorts were wet?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and wished he could vanish. His face burned and tears rolled.

qa.q: What could a teacher do when a class laughs at a child's mispronounced word?
qa.a: They could say that everyone is still learning words and let the child try again, as the teacher did with Akash.

grounding: Four small embarrassments (a laughed-at word, an accident in class, spilt juice, being made to stand) each meet a different response from classmates, teachers and a parent.
